title: What large language models know and what people think they know
abstract: Abstract As artificial intelligence systems, particularly large language models (LLMs), become increasingly integrated into decision-making processes, the ability to trust their outputs is crucial. To earn human trust, LLMs must be well calibrated such that they can accurately assess and communicate the likelihood of their predictions being correct. Whereas recent work has focused on LLMs’ internal confidence, less is understood about how effectively they convey uncertainty to users. Here we explore the calibration gap, which refers to the difference between human confidence in LLM-generated answers and the models’ actual confidence, and the discrimination gap, which reflects how well humans and models can distinguish between correct and incorrect answers. Our experiments with multiple-choice and short-answer questions reveal that users tend to overestimate the accuracy of LLM responses when provided with default explanations. Moreover, longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy. By adjusting LLM explanations to better reflect the models’ internal confidence, both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap narrowed, significantly improving user perception of LLM accuracy. These findings underscore the importance of accurate uncertainty communication and highlight the effect of explanation length in influencing user trust in artificial-intelligence-assisted decision-making environments.

claims.text: Users tend to overestimate the accuracy of LLM responses when provided with default explanations.
Longer LLM explanations increase user confidence without improving user discrimination between correct and incorrect answers.
Aligning uncertainty language in LLM explanations with internal model confidence narrows both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap.
LLM internal model confidence discriminates between correct and incorrect answers well above chance performance.
Human confidence based on default LLM explanations discriminates correct from incorrect answers only slightly better than random guessing.
Participants' self-assessed topic expertise does not significantly improve their ability to calibrate or discriminate LLM accuracy.

limitations.text: The evaluation focuses on specific question types involving small numbers of response choices (multiple choice) and short open-ended answers.
Modifying explanations based on internal uncertainty requires prompting the LLM twice rather than generating confidence-modified explanations in a single step.
Studies investigating how effectively LLMs convey uncertainty to human users and user confidence in LLM outputs are lacking.

future_work.text: Investigate the applicability of findings to longer open-ended questions across a broader range of scenarios.
Develop approaches to produce confidence-modified explanations in a single prompting step.
Investigate the fundamental causes of uncertainty miscommunication, such as RLHF preference biases or autoregressive choice-supportive biases.
